Guiding idea

The auth server issues the token. This service decides whether to trust it.

Follow the token from the browser, through Spring Security, into a method-level authorization decision — in a city that feels almost like a fairy tale.

Issuer → Validator → Authorization
1

The architecture: issuer over there, validator over here

The auth server runs on port 3000 and issues JWTs. The Cartel admin console runs on port 8080 and acts as a resource server that validates those JWTs before serving protected data.

1
LoginThe browser sends username and password to the auth server.
2
TokenThe auth server returns a signed JWT containing identity and scope.
3
Protected APIThe browser sends that JWT to port 8080 as a Bearer token.
4
Local validationSpring Security checks the signature and claims without calling port 3000.
5
AuthenticationA valid token becomes an authenticated principal inside Spring Security.
6
AuthorizationMethod security decides whether that authenticated user can run the endpoint.
“A fairy-tale town is no use unless you can still explain the security architecture clearly.”
Quiz hint

Be able to explain why there is no request-time arrow from the protected service back to the auth service. A signed token is designed to be independently verifiable by a service that already has the verification key material.

Are the swans still there?They are — and they make a surprisingly good reminder that a protected API can still be elegant while being strict about trust.
2

Start the protected service

The application itself is intentionally small. The interesting work happens in Spring Security configuration.

App.java 
package com.mcnz.cartel;

import org.springframework.boot.SpringApplication;
import org.springframework.boot.autoconfigure.SpringBootApplication;

@SpringBootApplication
public class App {

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        SpringApplication.run(App.class, args);
    }
}
Two services, two responsibilities. The auth server authenticates credentials and issues tokens. This application protects resources and validates tokens.
“He really does have a gift for profanity, doesn’t he?” In our case, the better habit is being just as emphatic about responsibilities: issuers issue, validators validate, and controllers authorize.
3

Reuse the user document and repository

The admin console reads the same MongoDB user documents. For this tutorial, the repository is simple because Spring Data provides the CRUD operations.

UserAccount.java 
package com.mcnz.cartel;

import org.springframework.data.annotation.Id;
import org.springframework.data.mongodb.core.mapping.Document;

@Document("users")
public class UserAccount {

    @Id
    private String username;

    private String passwordHash;
    private String roles;
    private String refreshTokenHash;
}
UserAccountRepository.java 
package com.mcnz.cartel;

import org.springframework.data.mongodb.repository.MongoRepository;

public interface UserAccountRepository
        extends MongoRepository<UserAccount, String> {
}
Security design note: returning the persistence entity directly is convenient for a classroom demo, but a real admin API should return a safe DTO that omits password hashes and refresh-token material.
The validation bridge

The token crosses services. The password does not.

Once a user has a valid access token, the protected API does not need the login password. It needs enough trusted information to validate the token and enforce authorization.

That is the quiet beauty of this lesson: the swans, the clocktower, the canals — and beneath it all, a resource server making a hard trust decision locally.

4

SecurityConfig.java — the mechanism that validates the JWT

This is the center of the lesson. Read it in two passes: first the HTTP security chain, then the JwtDecoder.

SecurityConfig.java 
package com.mcnz.cartel;

import java.nio.charset.StandardCharsets;

import javax.crypto.SecretKey;
import javax.crypto.spec.SecretKeySpec;

import org.springframework.context.annotation.Bean;
import org.springframework.context.annotation.Configuration;
import org.springframework.security.config.Customizer;
import org.springframework.security.config.annotation.method.configuration.EnableMethodSecurity;
import org.springframework.security.config.annotation.web.builders.HttpSecurity;
import org.springframework.security.config.http.SessionCreationPolicy;
import org.springframework.security.oauth2.core.DelegatingOAuth2TokenValidator;
import org.springframework.security.oauth2.core.OAuth2TokenValidator;
import org.springframework.security.oauth2.jose.jws.MacAlgorithm;
import org.springframework.security.oauth2.jwt.Jwt;
import org.springframework.security.oauth2.jwt.JwtAudienceValidator;
import org.springframework.security.oauth2.jwt.JwtDecoder;
import org.springframework.security.oauth2.jwt.JwtValidators;
import org.springframework.security.oauth2.jwt.NimbusJwtDecoder;
import org.springframework.security.web.SecurityFilterChain;

@Configuration
@EnableMethodSecurity
public class SecurityConfig {

    private static final String JWT_SECRET =
            "marcus-the-worm-has-a-secret-plot-to-get-jimbo-james-out-of-jail";

    private static final String JWT_ISSUER = "http://localhost:3000";
    private static final String JWT_AUDIENCE = "cartel-control";

    @Bean
    SecurityFilterChain securityFilterChain(HttpSecurity http) throws Exception {
        configureCsrf(http);
        configureSessions(http);
        configureAuthorization(http);
        configureJwt(http);
        return http.build();
    }

    private void configureCsrf(HttpSecurity http) throws Exception {
        http.csrf(csrf -> csrf.disable());
    }

    private void configureSessions(HttpSecurity http) throws Exception {
        http.sessionManagement(session ->
            session.sessionCreationPolicy(SessionCreationPolicy.STATELESS)
        );
    }

    private void configureAuthorization(HttpSecurity http) throws Exception {
        http.authorizeHttpRequests(auth -> {
            auth.requestMatchers("/", "/index.html", "/cartel/**",
                "/error", "/favicon.ico").permitAll();
            auth.requestMatchers("/api/cartel/**").authenticated();
            auth.anyRequest().permitAll();
        });
    }

    private void configureJwt(HttpSecurity http) throws Exception {
        http.oauth2ResourceServer(
            oauth -> oauth.jwt(Customizer.withDefaults())
        );
    }

    @Bean
    JwtDecoder jwtDecoder() {
        SecretKey secretKey = new SecretKeySpec(
            JWT_SECRET.getBytes(StandardCharsets.UTF_8),
            "HmacSHA256"
        );

        NimbusJwtDecoder decoder =
            NimbusJwtDecoder.withSecretKey(secretKey)
                .macAlgorithm(MacAlgorithm.HS256)
                .build();

        OAuth2TokenValidator<Jwt> issuerValidator =
            JwtValidators.createDefaultWithIssuer(JWT_ISSUER);

        OAuth2TokenValidator<Jwt> audienceValidator =
            new JwtAudienceValidator(JWT_AUDIENCE);

        decoder.setJwtValidator(
            new DelegatingOAuth2TokenValidator<>(
                issuerValidator,
                audienceValidator
            )
        );

        return decoder;
    }
}

Pass 1: the HTTP security chain

A
CSRF disabledThe protected API is being used as a stateless token-based service rather than a server-side browser session application.
B
Stateless sessionsSpring is told not to create or rely on an HTTP session for authentication state.
C
Route rulesStatic pages remain public while /api/cartel/** requires authentication.
D
Resource server modeoauth2ResourceServer(...jwt...) tells Spring Security to expect Bearer JWTs.

Pass 2: the JwtDecoder

1
Build the HMAC keyThe resource server uses the same shared secret that the auth server used to sign the token.
2
Require HS256NimbusJwtDecoder is configured for HMAC SHA-256, matching the issuer's signing algorithm.
3
Verify signatureIf header.payload was changed, the recalculated HMAC will not match the signature.
4
Validate issuerThe token must identify http://localhost:3000 as its issuer.
5
Validate audienceThe aud claim must contain cartel-control.
6
Create AuthenticationOnly after validation can Spring treat the token's subject and authorities as trusted security context.
“Do you have to?” In design terms: no, you do not have to trust every token. You verify the signature, the issuer, the audience, the expiry and the shape of the claims — and only then do you let it in.
Quiz hint

JWT validation is more than Base64-decoding the payload. Think about what proves the token was not changed and which claims prove the token was intended for this system.

It really is a fairy-tale town.Hard to imagine it not being somebody’s thing — especially when it comes wrapped around a lesson about local JWT verification, issuer checks and method security.
5

CartelController.java — authentication is not authorization

A valid token gets the caller through the first gate. Method security then asks whether this particular caller is allowed to run this operation.

CartelController.java 
package com.mcnz.cartel;

import java.util.List;

import org.springframework.beans.factory.annotation.Autowired;
import org.springframework.security.access.prepost.PreAuthorize;
import org.springframework.web.bind.annotation.GetMapping;
import org.springframework.web.bind.annotation.RequestMapping;
import org.springframework.web.bind.annotation.RestController;

@RestController
@RequestMapping("/api/cartel")
public class CartelController {

    @Autowired
    private UserAccountRepository users;

    @PreAuthorize(
        "hasAuthority('SCOPE_admin') or authentication.name == 'marcus'"
    )
    @GetMapping("/users")
    public List<UserAccount> users() {
        return users.findAll();
    }
}

The endpoint requires an authenticated JWT because of the URL rule in SecurityConfig. Then @PreAuthorize applies a finer-grained rule: the caller must either have the SCOPE_admin authority or have the authenticated name marcus.

Why SCOPE_admin? Spring Security's JWT support commonly maps token scope values into authorities prefixed with SCOPE_. A token carrying admin in its scope can therefore satisfy hasAuthority("SCOPE_admin").
Quiz hint

Keep the two questions separate: “Is this token valid and who is the caller?” is authentication. “May this caller invoke this method?” is authorization.

Browser to API

The browser is the courier.

First it gets the JWT from the auth server. Then it presents that JWT to the resource server as a Bearer token. That is all the protected API needs in order to validate the request locally.

And yes — the swans are still there.

6

The browser carries the JWT between the two services

The supplied login page calls the auth server on port 3000, stores the returned token in sessionStorage, and redirects into the Cartel UI.

Bearer request from the browser 
const token = sessionStorage.getItem("cartelAccessToken");

const response = await fetch("/api/cartel/users", {
  headers: {
    "Authorization": `Bearer ${token}`
  }
});
Important: the Bearer token goes to the protected API. The username and password do not need to be resent on each request.
7

Local and production MongoDB configuration

Like the auth service, the admin console can use the local MongoDB database in development or MongoDB Atlas remotely.

application.properties 
server.port=8080
spring.application.name=cartel-admin-console
server.error.include-message=always

spring.profiles.active=prod

#---
spring.config.activate.on-profile=local

spring.data.mongodb.host=localhost
spring.data.mongodb.port=27018
spring.data.mongodb.database=cartel-user-database

#---
spring.config.activate.on-profile=prod

spring.data.mongodb.uri=mongodb+srv://jimbo_db_user:${MONGODB_PASSWORD}@cartel-cluster.rhnc2gc.mongodb.net/cartel-user-database?appName=cartel-cluster

The key idea is not that JWT validation requires MongoDB — it does not. The database is used because this API returns and will later manage user records. Signature verification itself is performed locally from the JWT and the configured secret.

8

Test the complete validation path

Start both applications, obtain a JWT from the auth service, then send that token to the protected endpoint.

curl 
# get a JWT from the auth server on port 3000
curl -X POST http://localhost:3000/auth/login \
  -H "Content-Type: application/x-www-form-urlencoded" \
  -d "username=marcus&password=abc123"

# then call the protected API on port 8080
curl http://localhost:8080/api/cartel/users \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN"
401
Authentication failed

Typical causes: no token, malformed token, invalid signature, expired token, wrong issuer or wrong audience.

403
Authorization failed

The token can be valid but the authenticated user still may not satisfy the method-level role/scope rule.

Quiz hint

A valid signature is necessary, but it is not the entire authorization decision. Be ready to distinguish “the JWT is invalid” from “the JWT is valid, but this user lacks permission.”

9

Go forth: turn the read-only console into a real admin API

You now have the important security boundary in place. The best next exercise is to extend the API rather than merely add more explanation.

Update users

Add PUT or PATCH functionality for safe profile fields. Decide which roles are allowed to edit which fields.

Delete users

Add DELETE support with explicit authorization rules and a clear response when the user does not exist.

Add and remove roles

Create an admin-only endpoint for changing the roles assigned to an existing user.

Search and filter

Support looking up users by username or role instead of always returning the full registry.

Introduce safe DTOs

Stop returning the persistence entity directly so password hashes and refresh-token state never appear in API responses.

Think about token freshness

If you change a user's roles in MongoDB, an already-issued JWT still contains its old claims until another token is issued.

A useful design question: when an administrator changes someone's roles, should the change take effect immediately, or only when that user receives a new access token? Your answer pushes you directly into refresh-token lifecycle, revocation and shorter access-token expiries.
10

What you should be able to explain now

If you can narrate this flow without reading the code, you understand the security architecture rather than just the Spring annotations.

✓
JWT issuerThe auth server authenticates credentials and signs the token.
✓
JWT validatorThe resource server independently verifies signature, issuer, audience and standard validity rules.
✓
PrincipalA successfully validated token becomes trusted Authentication state inside Spring Security.
✓
AuthoritiesScope values become authorities that method security can inspect.
✓
401 vs 403Invalid identity proof is different from valid identity without permission.
✓
Next iterationExtend the protected API with safe CRUD and role-management operations.

Core question

What exactly happens between receiving Authorization: Bearer ... and allowing users() to execute?

Same canals. Bigger horizons. And then it hits you: if you had to spend all eternity in this place, it would be beautiful, haunting, and maybe a little unbearable — which is a fitting mood for thinking about revocation, CRUD, and role management after a long day with JWTs.
